query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-element near-equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles, higher noble‐metal content accelerates high-temperature surface segregation and sintering, thereby compromising structural and chemical stability under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions, while lower noble-metal content maintains a more uniform phase and better performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution nanoparticles with near-equiatomic multi-element compositions, initially exhibiting a random, single-phase structure under controlled synthesis conditions.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled-variable experiments where the noble-metal content is systematically varied while keeping other synthesis parameters constant, followed by in situ high-temperature XRD and catalytic/thermoelectric performance tests.
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated service regimes: catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K, in an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize extraneous oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface segregation leading to the formation of noble-metal-rich clusters that promote localized sintering and phase instability.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, atoms in the nanoparticles become mobile; noble metals, due to their distinct diffusion kinetics, preferentially migrate to the surface. This migration reduces the overall mixing stability of the solid solution, thereby promoting sintering and potential phase separation. Nanoparticles with a lower noble-metal concentration experience less segregation, thus better retaining their intended single-phase structure and performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with increased noble-metal content will show shifts and broadening in in situ high-temperature XRD peaks (indicative of structural changes), observable surface segregation in TEM/EDS, and degraded catalytic performance (e.g., reduced conversion rates) compared to lower noble-metal content nanoparticles, which will largely preserve their phase and performance up to the specified service temperatures.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with a moderate, baseline noble-metal content known from prior work to form stable solid solutions at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesized mechanism is expected to dominate under high-temperature regimes (773–1923 K) in controlled atmospheres; however, uncontrollable environmental factors (such as oxygen impurities) or very low/alloying extremes may alter the outcomes. The exact threshold of noble-metal content inducing instability remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: While the direction of the effect is supported by known diffusion and segregation principles, the quantitative thresholds (noble-metal concentration at which instability becomes significant) and the detailed kinetic parameters remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles with systematically varied noble-metal contents while keeping other synthesis parameters unchanged. Subject each sample to in situ high-temperature XRD and TEM analysis during catalytic testing (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric assessments (473–1923 K). Compare structural integrity (phase retention, peak shifts, and broadening) and catalytic performance metrics across the samples.
measurements: XRD: peak positions, intensities, and broadening before and after high-temperature exposure
TEM/EDS: imaging and chemical mapping to detect surface segregation and sintering
Catalytic performance: reaction conversion rates or kinetic parameters measured in a flow reactor
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increased noble-metal content does not lead to statistically significant changes in XRD patterns (e.g., no notable peak shifts or broadening), no observable surface segregation via TEM/EDS, and does not correlate with a decrease in catalytic/thermoelectric performance compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

chosen.technique: in situ high-temperature XRD coupled with flow reactor catalytic tests

chosen.why: This move directly targets the untested condition by isolating the impact of noble-metal concentration on the structural and chemical stability of multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles under realistic service regimes. It offers a clear mechanistic hypothesis—if variations in noble-metal content drive differential surface segregation or sintering behaviors at high temperatures, measurable differences in in situ XRD patterns and catalytic performance will emerge relative to a baseline. This is a standard and feasible experimental intervention in materials science to resolve conflicting explanations regarding the role of noble metals on nanoparticle stability.
